title: Common paediatric medical conditions
objectives: Recognise neonatal sepsis and SIRS criteria and state first-hour actions.
Manage febrile neutropenia in a child on chemotherapy stepwise.
Correct dehydration and common electrolyte emergencies with safe rates.
body_md:
### Why this area matters

Surgeons get examined on the medicine that kills surgical babies: sepsis, fluids, neutropenic fever. These are protocol questions — the marks go to order, doses and thresholds, not essays.

### Sepsis and SIRS

Neonatal sepsis presents vaguely — temperature instability, feed intolerance, lethargy, apnoea, mottling. Blood cultures first, then broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour, glucose and perfusion support alongside. Legacy SIRS criteria (temperature, heart and respiratory rate, white cells) organise the answer even as definitions evolve; MODS is the same story across two or more failing systems. Source control is the surgical contribution — drain the collection, remove the dead bowel, debride the wound.

### Febrile neutropenia

Fever in a neutropenic child on chemotherapy is an emergency by definition: cultures, then empiric anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam immediately. Add vancomycin for line infection, MRSA risk or instability; add antifungals for persistent fever beyond 4–7 days. Risk-stratify (MASCC-style thinking adapted to children), watch the absolute neutrophil count nadir timing against the chemo calendar, and use G-CSF per protocol, not panic.

### Fluids and electrolytes

Resuscitate with isotonic boluses and reassess; maintenance follows Holliday-Segar thinking adjusted for neonates; replace ongoing losses. Hyponatraemia correct slowly, hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia act fast on the heart — state ECG changes and treatment thresholds and the examiner stops reading critically.

### How it is asked

As sub-parts inside surgical questions (sepsis after NEC, fluids around pyloric stenosis) or standalone protocols. Write in numbered steps with doses and timeframes.
